newsitem.title: USA: Appeals Court upholds Tailhook ruling against Hilton.
newsitem.headline: Appeals Court upholds Tailhook ruling against Hilton.

text.p: A federal appeals court upheld a $5 million judgment Friday against the Las Vegas Hilton and its parent company in a suit by a former Navy lieutenant who was sexually harassed at a pilots' convention.

The 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in San Francisco affirmed a Nevada federal court jury's decision in favor of former Navy helicopter pilot Paula Coughlin, saying substantial evidence supported the jury's finding that Hilton Hotels Corp. "acted with a conscious disregard for the rights or safety of hotel guests" over the incident.

Coughlin was one of more than 80 women alleged to have been groped and sexually molested as they ran a gauntlet of drunken male pilots in a hallway of the Las Vegas Hilton during the annual meeting of the Tailhook Association of Navy and Marine aviators in September 1991.
The scandal rocked the Navy and resulted in disciplinary action against 40 officers, including three admirals.
Coughlin -- the first woman to complain of assault -- suffered psychological problems related to the attack and eventually had to resign her commission because of the problems, the court record said.

Coughlin sued the Tailhook Association, Las Vegas Hilton Corp. and its parent, Hilton Hotels Corp., alleging both hotel companies had acted with conscious disregard for safety standards. The association settled with Coughlin for $400,000 but a trial of her claims against the Las Vegas Hilton and Hilton Hotels Corp. went forward.

Evidence was presented at the trial showing that the Las Vegas Hilton knew about convention-related assaults as early as 1988, including an attack on a young woman that was similar to that on Coughlin, the appeals court's ruling said.
"The evidence indicated that Hilton Hotels Corp.'s response to the earlier incident was insufficient to ensure the safety of female guests during the 1991 Tailhook convention," it said.
The jury found the Las Vegas Hilton and Hilton Hotels Corp. negligent and awarded Coughlin $1.7 million in compensatory damages and punitive damages totaling $4.9 million.

The Nevada district court reduced the compensatory damages by $400,000 -- the amount of Coughlin's settlement with the Tailhook Association -- before applying a Nevada law limiting punitive damages to three times compensatory damages. The court reduced punitive damages to a total of $3.9 million.

The Las Vegas Hilton and Hilton Hotels Corp. appealed, contending that the evidence was insufficient to support an award of punitive damages. They also sought reversal of the jury verdict because one of the jurors did not disclose his criminal record.

The appeals court said the evidence presented at trial was sufficient for a reasonable jury to conclude that Hilton Hotels Corp. "was aware of the probable dangerous consequences of its conduct, and willfully and deliberately failed to avoid them."
It also said there was nothing to indicate that the juror who failed to disclose his criminal record was biased against Hilton and therefore a new trial was not warranted.

Coughlin also appealed the original verdict, saying the district court was wrong to deduct the $400,000 settlement before calculating punitive damages. The Appeals Court referred this question to the Nevada Supreme Court to decide.

Marc Grossman, a spokesman for Hilton Hotels Corp., said: "We are disappointed with the court's decision and we are exploring our options." Coughlin's attorney Nancy Stagg said Coughlin was "really pleased" with the ruling.
